reasoning: Both reviewers independently converge on the same fundamental diagnosis: this manuscript makes specific quantitative claims (20% IoU improvement, 30% processing-time reduction) about enhancements to MediaPipe for pose estimation, but provides essentially no empirical evidence, no defined methodology, no dataset, no baseline specification, no actual results tables or figures, and no identifiable intervention. reflection_a.defense_for_self:
My RETRACTION-WORTHY ratings are not overstated because they map exactly onto the stated standard: the paper’s central conclusions cannot be supported by the data as presented. This manuscript does not merely have weak reporting or missing polish. It is missing the empirical and methodological substrate required for its headline claims. The core claims are: (i) the authors made specific enhancements to MediaPipe, (ii) those enhancements improved accuracy and robustness, and (iii) they reduced processing time relative to baseline methods. For each of those claims, the paper withholds the indispensable information needed to determine whether the claim is true.

Why Findings 1, 2, 3, and 6 are genuinely RETRACTION-WORTHY:

1) Unsupported primary performance claims due to absent results are RETRACTION-WORTHY, not merely MAJOR-REVISION.
The manuscript makes explicit quantitative claims such as a 20% IoU increase and 30% processing-time reduction, and invokes missing Table 1 and Figures 1–3 as support. But the actual evidence is absent. That means the paper’s conclusions are not just weakly evidenced; they are evidence-free within the document. A scientific paper exists to present the data supporting its conclusions. If the data are not there, the conclusions cannot be supported by the paper as published. This is precisely the threshold for RETRACTION-WORTHY under the provided rubric: the central conclusions cannot be supported by the data as presented.

This is stronger than the other reviewer’s framing because even calling this a 'reporting omission' understates the defect. The paper is built around comparative empirical claims. When the comparative data are missing altogether, there is no valid inferential chain left. The defect does not affect a secondary analysis or a robustness check; it destroys the evidentiary basis for the main message. A revision could, in theory, add results, but that concession is not the severity test. The severity test asks what follows if the error is confirmed in the paper as presented. If confirmed, the article’s primary conclusions are unsupported and would need withdrawal or rejection, not merely editorial polishing.

2) Undefined intervention/proposed enhancement is RETRACTION-WORTHY because there is no identifiable object of evaluation.
The paper claims that 'refined algorithms' and 'advanced neural network architectures' improve MediaPipe, but never specifies what was changed. This is not just an incomplete methods section. It means there is no defined treatment, model, or intervention whose effects can be assessed. Without a concretely described modification, one cannot tell what system produced the claimed gains, whether any gains belong to MediaPipe modifications at all, whether the claims arise from preprocessing, post-processing, hardware differences, threshold tuning, or a different model entirely.

The other reviewer labels this MAJOR-REVISION; I maintain RETRACTION-WORTHY because the undefined intervention invalidates attribution of the core contribution. The manuscript’s central claim is not simply 'we built a curl counter' or 'we used MediaPipe.' It is that specific enhancements to MediaPipe yield superior pose-estimation performance. If the enhancements are not actually described, the central scientific contribution is untestable and therefore unsupported. This is not a repairable side issue; it voids the paper’s main causal/comparative claim as written.

3) Absence of dataset, annotation protocol, and ground truth is RETRACTION-WORTHY because the accuracy metrics are uninterpretable without them.
The manuscript reports accuracy-oriented metrics such as MSE and IoU, but gives no valid ground-truth source, no annotation procedure, no benchmark dataset, no number of subjects, no frame counts, no labeling process, and no test split. For pose estimation, metrics only acquire meaning relative to known target coordinates, masks, boxes, or otherwise defined reference standards. If ground truth is unspecified, then the reported accuracy values are not merely irreproducible; they are uninterpretable. One cannot know what quantity was compared to what.

This goes beyond ordinary missing detail. In pose estimation, the entire empirical claim of improvement rests on comparing predictions against a reference. If the reference is absent or undefined, then the numerical claims have no scientific meaning. The paper’s primary conclusion of improved pose accuracy therefore cannot be sustained. That is RETRACTION-WORTHY by definition.

6) Undefined baseline comparison is RETRACTION-WORTHY because superiority claims require a specified comparator under matched conditions.
The paper repeatedly claims superiority over baseline MediaPipe and 'traditional models,' yet does not specify the baseline version, model configuration, thresholds, hardware, runtime environment, resolution, or fairness controls. When a paper’s central conclusion is comparative superiority, an unspecified comparator nullifies the conclusion. 'Better than baseline' is not a meaningful scientific statement unless the baseline is concretely identified and evaluated under comparable conditions.

The other reviewer treated related concerns as RETRACTION-WORTHY in part; I go further in defending this as independently RETRACTION-WORTHY because comparative claims are logically impossible to verify without a comparator. This is not analogous to an omitted hyperparameter that affects reproducibility but leaves the result conceptually interpretable. Here, the omitted comparator definition erases the very relation the paper is claiming. Without a defined baseline, there is no valid claim of improvement.

Defense against alternative framings:

A) 'These are just missing details that could be fixed in revision.'
That framing confuses fixability with severity. Many retraction-level defects are theoretically fixable by rerunning analyses or providing omitted materials, but the severity rubric here is explicit: if confirmed, do the central conclusions fail as presented? Yes. This paper asks the reader to accept quantitative superiority claims with no visible supporting data, no defined intervention, no defined dataset/ground truth, and no defined baseline. As published, those claims are fundamentally unsupported. That is not a request for cleaner reporting; it is a failure of evidentiary sufficiency.

B) 'The code repository may contain the missing specifics.'
A manuscript cannot outsource its core scientific validity to an unspecified external repository, especially when the paper itself does not map code to experiments, parameters, datasets, or the exact evaluation pipeline. A paper’s conclusions must be justified in the paper. Otherwise, peer review cannot evaluate the work actually claimed. The existence of code does not cure missing experimental evidence or undefined methodology in the manuscript.

C) 'Perhaps the missing tables/figures were dropped accidentally in formatting.'
If that happened, it still supports my severity assessment under the rubric applied to the manuscript as presented. The results section is effectively empty of evidence while still making strong quantitative claims. If a production error removed all supporting data for the main conclusions, the paper in its presented form remains unsupported. That is exactly the kind of failure that warrants rejection or withdrawal until corrected; it is not a minor issue.

D) 'Undefined metrics and absent train/test details are only MAJOR-REVISION, so why are some neighboring findings RETRACTION-WORTHY?'
Because there is a principled distinction. Ambiguous metric formulation (e.g., unclear MSE aggregation) could, in theory, still correspond to a valid but poorly reported evaluation. Likewise, train/test leakage is a serious possibility that could alter conclusions, but the present manuscript does not provide enough to prove leakage occurred. Those are classic MAJOR-REVISION findings. By contrast, absent results, undefined intervention, missing ground truth/dataset, and undefined baseline directly remove the logical basis for the central claims. Those are not 'possible sources of bias'; they are direct failures of support.

Why my serious assessments should prevail over the alternative reviewer’s softer framing on the intervention finding:
The second reviewer rates the undefined method as MAJOR-REVISION. I disagree because the paper’s novelty claim is the method. If the method is not actually specified, there is no scientific contribution to evaluate. The paper then collapses into an unverified assertion that some unspecified changes produced some unspecified gains on some unspecified data against some unspecified baseline. At that point the problem is not merely non-reproducibility. It is non-identifiability of the thing being claimed. A central claim about efficacy of an undefined intervention cannot be supported.

Likewise, my RETRACTION-WORTHY assessment for the missing dataset/ground truth should stand. The other reviewer also flags this severely, but my reasoning is stronger: accuracy metrics in pose estimation are not ancillary; they are ontologically dependent on a reference target. Without one, the metrics are not just impossible to reproduce, they are scientifically meaningless. That crosses the threshold from 'needs more detail' to 'cannot support conclusion.'

For the remaining findings, my gradation is deliberate and defensible:
- IoU misuse is MAJOR-REVISION, not RETRACTION-WORTHY, because there is a narrow possibility the authors used a valid but unreported region-based or keypoint-derived IoU formulation.
- MSE ambiguity is MAJOR-REVISION because the metric might be salvageable if correctly defined.
- Missing train/test protocol is MAJOR-REVISION because leakage is plausible but not shown.
- Task conflation is MAJOR-REVISION because it risks overgeneralization but does not automatically nullify every result.
- Hard-threshold curl logic is MINOR because it weakens one application but does not, by itself, break the entire paper.
- Missing robustness operationalization, sample size omissions, absent hardware details, and lack of inferential statistics are MAJOR-REVISION because each could materially change interpretation but does not alone prove the main claims false.
- Manuscript integrity problems are MAJOR-REVISION because they substantially undermine trust and coherence but are not, standing alone, conclusive proof that the numerical claims are fabricated.

In sum: my severities are anchored to whether the paper’s main conclusions can stand on the evidence actually provided. For four findings, the answer is unequivocally no. Those findings are properly RETRACTION-WORTHY.

findings_i_still_defend.finding: The cited code repository may help reproducibility, but the manuscript does not map the code to the claimed experiments, parameter settings, datasets, or exact evaluation pipeline.
findings_i_still_defend.reason: Helpful but secondary reproducibility issue; not enough on its own to change the paper’s conclusions.

new_errors_noticed: The manuscript’s claim of a 'new benchmark' is especially problematic because no benchmark definition is provided: no task protocol, no dataset composition, no evaluation script, and no leaderboard-style comparator set. This is not just hype language; it is an unsupported institutional claim.

The paper appears to slide between evaluating pose estimation quality and evaluating an exercise-repetition counter. Those are distinct endpoints. Improvement in repetition counting does not establish improved landmark localization accuracy, robustness, or runtime for general pose estimation.

There is no evidence of any ablation isolating which alleged enhancement produced the reported gains. Even if some result existed, the paper would still fail to support the causal attribution that the named modifications caused the improvement.

The manuscript does not define whether inference is single-person or multi-person pose estimation, yet claims broad applicability. That omission matters because MediaPipe performance, evaluation design, and runtime differ substantially across those settings.
No calibration of camera geometry, viewpoint variation, or coordinate system is described, which is especially important if angle estimation and MSE over landmarks are central outcomes.

The paper does not specify whether processing-time measurements include image capture, preprocessing, model inference, rendering, or post-processing. This makes the runtime claim even less interpretable than I initially stated.

reflection_b.defense_for_self: My severity ratings are not over-stated but reflect the minimal threshold for retraction as defined: the central conclusions cannot be supported by the data as presented. The other reviewer's rating pattern, while also severe, diffuses responsibility across too many 'MAJOR-REVISION' items, allowing the paper's core fallacies to be obscured as mere reporting deficiencies. I stand by my classification because each RETRACTION-WORTHY finding strikes at the empirical foundation of the paper in a way that no amount of revision can salvage without starting over. Specifically: (1) The absence of a described dataset means there is no referent for any accuracy claim—this is not a missing table, it is missing the phenomenon under study. A revision cannot insert a dataset retroactively. (2) The missing tables and figures are not formatting gaps; they are the evacuation of the results section. Claims of numerical improvement without any numerical output are vacuous by definition—no revision can conjure data that was never collected. (3) The baseline comparison is undefined, so the central claim of 'improvement' has no anchor. (4) The methodological description is so sparse that the 'intervention'—the alleged enhancements to MediaPipe—is a black box. Without knowing what was actually done, no reviewer or reader can assess whether the method is valid, let alone reproducible. These are not 'fixable' with a revision; they would require an entirely new submission with complete experimental apparatus. My confidence (0.95) was slightly lower than the other reviewer's (0.98), reflecting a conservative acknowledgment that the paper *might* be an unusually sloppy draft of a real study, but the pattern of missing data, fabricated references, and incoherent methodology makes that extremely unlikely.
severity_i_now_upgrade: The use of IoU without justification — I now agree with the other reviewer that this is potentially RETRACTION-WORTHY, not MAJOR-REVISION. If the authors applied a segmentation/detection metric to a keypoint task without defining a mapping (e.g., bounding boxes from keypoints, heatmap thresholding), then the reported '20% IoU improvement' is not just poorly reported—it is mathematically meaningless. A claim that cannot be defined is not an empirical claim; it is a fabrication by metric misuse. This is a separate, independent reason the central conclusions are unsupported, warranting retraction.
findings_i_still_defend: Finding 1 (No dataset described) — RETRACTION-WORTHY. The other reviewer agrees this is RETRACTION-WORTHY (their finding 3). This is the strongest, most consequential finding. Without a dataset, the paper is not a scientific report; it is a narrative.

Finding 2 (Missing tables/figures) — RETRACTION-WORTHY. The other reviewer's finding 1 identifies the same issue but calls it 'unsupported claims' and rates it RETRACTION-WORTHY — we agree. The paper literally provides no data output. This is not a missing appendix; it is an empty results section.

Finding 3 (Unsubstantiated performance claims without statistical context) — RETRACTION-WORTHY. The other reviewer's findings 1, 6, and 12 collectively support this. The claims are not 'imprecise'—they are assertions floating without evidence. No confidence intervals, no error bars, no test conditions. These are not scientific claims; they are marketing copy.

Finding 5 (Fabricated/incomplete references) — MAJOR-REVISION. The other reviewer's finding 14 flags the same placeholder/reference integrity problems as 'MAJOR-REVISION'. I stand by MAJOR-REVISION because: fabricated references are indeed a serious ethical breach, but a retraction would be warranted only if the literature claims are central to the paper's novelty justification. In this paper, the literature review is tangential (the paper's failure is in results, not in citing prior work). However, if upon investigation the references are fabricated wholesale, this would escalate to an integrity-based retraction independent of the results. I retain MAJOR-REVISION because the paper's primary failure is evidentiary, not citational.

Finding 6 (MSE/IoU metric definition missing) — MAJOR-REVISION. The other reviewer's finding 4 treats IoU more severely (MAJOR-REVISION) and finding 5 treats MSE as MAJOR-REVISION. I now agree that IoU misuse could be RETRACTION-WORTHY (see upgrade above). For MSE, I keep MAJOR-REVISION: ambiguous metric definition makes interpretation difficult but does not alone prove the measurements were impossible—only that they are uninterpretable. If MSE was computed on normalized keypoint coordinates (standard practice), the definition gap is a reporting failure, not a fundamental impossibility.

Finding 7 (No quantitative breakdown by condition) — MINOR. The other reviewer's finding 11 raises robustness claims without operational definitions as MAJOR-REVISION. I disagree: the paper has *no* breakdown because it has *no* results at all. The absence of subgroup analysis is a minor concern only if the main results existed; here it is a secondary symptom of the primary data absence. I keep MINOR.
new_errors_noticed: The paper claims improvements in 'low light and partial occlusion' but never defines how these conditions were operationalized. If the authors filmed subjects walking in a dark room and called that 'low light,' there is no control condition (same scene with normal lighting) to isolate the variable. This is not just a reporting gap—it means the robustness conclusion is untestable even in principle from the described experiment. This should have been flagged as a separate RETRACTION-WORTHY finding or at least elevated to MAJOR-REVISION (which the other reviewer correctly did in their finding 11).

The manuscript conflates two distinct tasks: (a) general human pose estimation benchmark (improving MediaPipe's accuracy/speed across diverse conditions) and (b) a specific application (curl counter using shoulder-elbow-wrist angle). The paper then uses application-level success (detecting curls) as evidence for generic pose-estimation improvement. This is a category error: a curl counter can work well with poor pose estimation if the angle threshold happens to be robust to noise. The '20% IoU improvement' claim is presented as a pose-estimation metric, but the only described implementation is the curl counter. If the 20% number came from a different experiment (e.g., on standard benchmarks like COCO or MPII), the paper never says so. This conflation is a separate, independent flaw: the paper's central claim is about one thing, but the evidence (if any) is about another. This is potentially RETRACTION-WORTHY because the entire argument structure is mismatched.

The paper mentions 'advanced neural network architectures' but the only described processing pipeline is the pre-existing MediaPipe framework plus a rule-based angle threshold. There is no indication of any neural network training or modification. This is not just a lack of detail—it suggests the claimed 'enhancements' may not exist. The other reviewer's finding 2 flags this as RETRACTION-WORTHY, and I concur: if the method description contradicts the existence of the claimed innovation, the paper is not incomplete but fraudulent.

arbiter_raw.reasoning: Both reviewers independently converge on the same fundamental diagnosis: this manuscript makes specific quantitative claims (20% IoU improvement, 30% processing-time reduction) about enhancements to MediaPipe for pose estimation, but provides essentially no empirical evidence, no defined methodology, no dataset, no baseline specification, no actual results tables or figures, and no identifiable intervention. The paper's central conclusions cannot be supported by the data as presented because the data is absent. Multiple independent defects are each individually sufficient to render the core claims unsupported. After reflection, both reviewers maintained or strengthened their positions, with no downgrades. The pattern of placeholder references, generic author names, missing tables/figures, and vague methodology suggests the manuscript is either a template/placeholder or a fundamentally incomplete submission rather than a legitimate scientific report with fixable gaps.

findings.finding: Referenced Table 1 and Figures 1–3 containing experimental results are absent from the manuscript. No quantitative data, numerical comparisons, variance estimates, or statistical outputs are actually presented, yet the paper makes specific claims (20% IoU improvement, 30% speed reduction).
findings.justification: The paper's central conclusions are empirical and comparative. The complete absence of results data means there is zero evidential support for the headline claims within the manuscript. This is not a formatting gap—it is an empty results section with unsupported assertions. Both reviewers rated this RETRACTION-WORTHY and defended it through reflection.

findings.finding: No experimental dataset is described: no dataset name, number of subjects, number of frames, annotation protocol, ground-truth source, train/test split, resolution, frame rate, or ethical approval for human subjects.
findings.justification: Pose-estimation accuracy metrics (MSE, IoU) are defined relative to ground-truth annotations. Without any specification of the dataset or reference standard, the reported metrics are not merely irreproducible—they are uninterpretable. The central accuracy claims have no scientific meaning. Both reviewers rated this RETRACTION-WORTHY and strongly defended it.

findings.finding: The proposed 'enhancements' to MediaPipe are never concretely described. The paper uses vague phrases ('refined algorithms,' 'advanced neural network architectures') but provides no architecture modifications, training procedures, hyperparameters, loss functions, or optimization details. The only concrete processing described is a rule-based angle threshold for curl counting.
findings.justification: The paper's central novelty claim is that specific enhancements to MediaPipe produced measurable improvements. If the enhancements are undefined, there is no identifiable intervention to evaluate, attribute gains to, or replicate. The central scientific contribution is untestable. Reviewer A rated this RETRACTION-WORTHY and defended it vigorously; Reviewer B initially rated a related finding as MAJOR-REVISION but in reflection concurred that the absence of any described modification may indicate the claimed innovation does not exist.

findings.finding: The baseline comparison is completely undefined. The paper claims superiority over 'traditional models' and the 'baseline MediaPipe model' but specifies no version, configuration, hardware, thresholds, or matched conditions for comparison.
findings.justification: The paper's core claim is comparative improvement. Without an identified and specified comparator under matched conditions, the claim of superiority is logically empty. Both reviewers identified this as a critical defect; Reviewer A rated it RETRACTION-WORTHY, and Reviewer B's findings 3 and related reasoning support the same conclusion.

findings.finding: Several references use generic/placeholder author names ('Developer, B.,' 'Innovator, C.,' 'Researcher, A.') and journal placeholders ('[JOURNAL]'). Other references provide volume/page numbers but no journal name.
findings.justification: Fabricated or placeholder references are a serious integrity concern. However, the paper's primary failure is evidentiary rather than citational. If these are confirmed as fabricated, an independent ethics-based retraction would be warranted, but the severity here is assessed relative to the paper's empirical conclusions. Both reviewers rated this MAJOR-REVISION and maintained that rating through reflection.

findings.finding: IoU is used as a headline accuracy metric for keypoint-based pose estimation without any definition or justification of how IoU was adapted to this task. IoU is a segmentation/detection overlap metric, not a standard keypoint localization metric.
findings.justification: If IoU was applied without a valid mapping (e.g., bounding boxes, heatmaps), the '20% improvement' claim is mathematically meaningless. Reviewer B upgraded this toward RETRACTION-WORTHY in reflection; Reviewer A maintained MAJOR-REVISION, noting a narrow possibility of a valid but unreported formulation. Given the uncertainty, MAJOR-REVISION is appropriate—but this finding compounds the other RETRACTION-WORTHY issues.

findings.finding: MSE metric is insufficiently defined: unclear whether computed on normalized coordinates, pixel coordinates, angles, per-joint, or aggregated, with no normalization or subject-level aggregation strategy.
findings.justification: Ambiguous metric definition materially affects interpretation and comparability. Both reviewers rated this MAJOR-REVISION and maintained that through reflection.

findings.finding: The manuscript conflates two distinct tasks—general human pose estimation benchmarking and a specific curl-counter application—without clarifying which outcomes correspond to which task. Application-level success (counting curls) does not validate general pose-estimation accuracy claims.
findings.justification: This category error means the evidence (if any existed) would not support the breadth of the claims being made. Both reviewers identified this mismatch. Reviewer B in reflection suggested this could be RETRACTION-WORTHY due to the mismatched argument structure, but the finding alone does not definitively invalidate all conclusions—rather it inflates them. MAJOR-REVISION is appropriate.

findings.finding: No train/validation/test protocol or prevention of data leakage is described. It is unclear whether any model components were retrained, tuned on the evaluation set, or tested on overlapping subjects/scenes.
findings.justification: Potential data leakage could inflate performance, but leakage is not demonstrated from the manuscript alone. Both reviewers rated this MAJOR-REVISION.

findings.finding: Claims of robust performance under low light and partial occlusion are made without defining how those conditions were generated, measured, stratified, or analyzed. No control conditions are described.
findings.justification: Robustness claims are untestable without operational definitions. Both reviewers flagged this. It is a substantive methodological concern but secondary to the primary absence of any results.

findings.finding: No sample size, number of videos/frames, participant demographics, or number of repeated trials is reported.
findings.justification: Prevents assessment of power, reliability, and representativeness. Material concern but secondary to the complete absence of results data.

findings.finding: Computational efficiency claims (30% speed reduction) are uninterpretable because no hardware, software environment, device type, batch size, image resolution, or measurement protocol is specified.
findings.justification: Runtime claims are meaningless without context. Could materially change speed conclusions.

findings.finding: The manuscript asserts 'significant enhancements' and 'new benchmark' without any inferential statistics, confidence intervals, or uncertainty estimates.
findings.justification: Strong comparative language without statistical support is methodologically serious, but absence of significance testing alone is not automatically fatal.

findings.finding: Serious manuscript integrity problems: placeholder text ([JOURNAL]), incomplete/corrupted references with generic author names, abrupt topic shifts, duplicated or misplaced passages, and OCR-like fragmentation throughout.
findings.justification: These defects substantially undermine confidence that the manuscript represents a coherent, completed study. Reviewer A considered upgrading to RETRACTION-WORTHY if the pattern reflects a template-generated or fabricated manuscript. While strongly concerning, this finding alone is classified as MAJOR-REVISION; combined with the RETRACTION-WORTHY findings above, it reinforces the overall assessment.

findings.finding: The angle-based curl counter uses hard thresholds (>160°, <30°) with no justification, calibration, or cross-subject/viewpoint validation.
findings.justification: Weakens the application sub-component but would not independently invalidate the paper's main claims if those claims were otherwise supported.

findings.finding: The cited code repository is not mapped to the claimed experiments, parameter settings, datasets, or evaluation pipeline in the manuscript.
findings.justification: Standard reproducibility concern. A manuscript must justify its conclusions internally; external code alone cannot substitute for missing experimental evidence.
